quote: den största förändringen skedde 1870 då huset fick fristående flyglar, som ritades av arkitekten Adolf W. Edelsvärd.

Several rebuilds about 1700, among them today's sandstone street portal and new interiors.

The attic was fitted out in 1855-56, and the street front got decoration of its day at the same time.
The cellar and ground floor were rebuilt in 1912 to take shop windows.

Cellar card (1940, 1958; eye-checked): marked medieval, two large vaults under the old gateway; the courtyard wing's cellar has none. The 1983 facade card (SSM_DOK_000636) notes medieval-type anchors, brick perhaps late 1500s.

The museum's card (eye-checked): two medieval stone houses on this plot, medieval masonry four and three storeys high in the old courtyard facade, medieval niches in their cellars. The cannonball corner house.

quote: Nuvarande huset i kvarteret Ceres byggdes på 1700-talet

The museum's card: medieval masonry three storeys high toward the lane and Baggensgatan and four toward the courtyard; the medieval house took the plot's whole width on Baggensgatan, with medieval openings. No year.

quote: Bebyggelsen med den lägre tvåvåningsbyggnaden i hörnet Munkbrogatan 11 / Schönfeldts gränd 12 motsvarar idag fortfarande 1872 års om- och nybyggnad.

A 1600s rebuild of the medieval house added the facade anchors and the carved stone portal; the sheet dates that portal to the second half of the 1600s, so the rebuild is read as then.
Raised by two storeys after an 1804 application (first drawn for one), which gave the house its present five-storey height; the sheet heads this the 1804 rebuild.

In the later 1600s the house was extended by four window bays to the south-west (both reports).
A fourth storey (applied for in 1837) and a house on the former courtyard (1838) stood by 1839, per the fire insurance.

Cellar-only: the 1940 cellar survey finds the whole cellar of the southern of the two joined plots medieval, with niches and a medieval cellar stair; the northern plot shows a small medieval patch. Nothing above ground is dated.

quote: hade sin första ägare i det då nybyggda huset (Västerlånggatan 77/ Prästgatan 76) år 1600

The museum's card: foundations of two medieval houses toward Västerlånggatan, a large cellar mostly intact from several medieval periods; the 1979 drawings (p. 54) record medieval doors and windows in the street front's two lowest storeys.

Raised a storey, old roof removed, in 1877-78 (applied for 1876). Wikipedia gives 1876, KulturNav 1874; Wikipedia's 1864 new house on the whole block conflicts with the surviving 1600s and medieval fabric.

The museum's 2003 masonry record of this house: a half-timbered house in the 1600s, first called a stone house about 1720, and the brickwork fits a rebuild in stone then. The cellar's stone walls may be older.

The museum's card for the corner house Köpmangatan 1B / Själagårdsgatan 1 (surveys 1940, 1968-70): two medieval houses inside today's volume, their walls kept from the cellar up to the fourth storey. No year, so medieval.

The museum's card (1970-71) for this property, given there as Själagårdsgatan 7: medieval walls in a three-storey street house and a four-storey medieval courtyard house kept whole. The footprint runs from the street to that courtyard house.
The museum's 1985 note: medieval-type walls in monk bond kept four storeys high in the south facade (three in the north facade, card p. 1). The article says nothing about this house.
Same note: the top storey and the attic were built in the 1830s (it cites the building board's file of 1834).

The museum's 1981-82 note on this house (Österlånggatan 3 / Telegrafgränd 5): medieval walls in monk bond in the ground floor of the south facade, perhaps higher; the 1940 cellar card (SSM_DOK_000272 p. 3) marks medieval walls too.

quote: har ett enkelt äldre utförande som till stor del härrör från 1760-talet
note: Swedish Wikipedia: the plain street facade is largely from the 1760s (shop window 1800s, changes 1960s). A facade date, so shown as a later rebuild, not the build year.

The 1979 inventory: medieval walls in the street house's cellar and in the ground-floor gateway, and a stone house on the plot by the 1500s; Swedish Wikipedia speaks of a 500-year history. The east courtyard house is the other footprint.
Same inventory: the street house was rebuilt about 1770 to drawings of 1768, with a fourth storey and a new room layout (PDF pp. 13-15); the courtyard house had been rebuilt and raised from 1754.
The street house's rear wing, inside this footprint, was probably begun after 1630 and raised in stages through the 1600s, judging by its wall anchors. Its north part keeps medieval masonry (p. 6).

The west courtyard house, inside this footprint, was extended east and given a fourth storey and new interiors under the owner who bought in 1750, before the 1768 drawings. The 1979 inventory says from 1754.
The street house's present ground-floor shop front, with its door and large window, dates from the 1880s.

In the early-1980s refurbishment the street house's fire-damaged attic became a flat with three new dormers; the sheet dates the dormers to the 1980s. The west courtyard house's attic flat was enlarged later in the decade.

Several old plots in one footprint. The museum's cards: a medieval house three storeys high at Stora Hoparegränd 5 (1968-70, p. 6), and one or two medieval stone houses kept up to the fourth floor on the Österlånggatan corner (p. 14).

quote: Det förmodas att 1655 även är byggnadsåret.
note: Swedish Wikipedia: the Stora Hoparegränd 5 house is a 1600s house with a portal stone reading ANNO 1655, thought to be its building year. The museum found medieval walls in the same house, so 1655 shows as the later rebuild.

The 1984 inventory (BY-NC-SA, register-linked): the house went up in 1769-70 where three older houses of medieval origin stood; their walls survive in the cellars. Little changed since 1770. The museum's card (SSM_DOK_000277 p. 2) agrees: drawings dated 1769.

The museum's 1982 facade note: two houses merged in the 1750s. The small east one keeps medieval walls nearly three storeys up; the larger west one is mostly 1600s brickwork with mid-1600s anchors (p. 3). Medieval origin shown.
Same note: the thorough rebuild of 1876 (the ground-floor room lost its vault then).

Two old plots on Köpmangatan. The museum's cards: medieval cellars of several houses (pp. 36, 39), and the courtyard facade of the Köpmangatan 4 house keeps medieval walls three storeys high (1941, p. 39). No source gives a year.

quote: ägdes under medeltiden av Själagården och 1487 blev den bebyggd
note: The corner plot, owned by the Själagården in the Middle Ages, was built on in 1487; the article's next step is the first major rebuild in the 1680s, and it says every house in the block keeps medieval walls. Shown as built 1487.

quote: Den första större om- och påbyggnaden av fastigheten utfördes på 1680 av handelsmannen Olof Hansson Törne
note: First major rebuild and raising, with the säteri roof that survives. The article says 'på 1680'; read as about 1680, the 1680s.

quote: Sitt nuvarande utseende med de stora välvda skyltfönstren fick huset mellan åren 1907 och 1909
note: Present look with the large arched shop windows, by Dorph & Höög.
Rebuilt in 1852: the northern of the two stairs went, a stone stair up to the attic was added and two rooms were made in the attic.
The facade was redressed in the 1880s with heavy moulded surrounds, then the fashion; the rebuild of 1907-09 stripped this 1800s decoration off again.

The museum's 2004 masonry record after the 2002 fire: medieval walls in all three storeys of the facade, in the west and south walls up to the attic, and in both cellar rooms. Roof rebuilt after 1817, top-floor ceiling raised in 1900.

The museum's 2000 facade record of the Västerlånggatan front: medieval walls in monk bond from the second storey to just above the third, with the medieval house corner; larger windows put in during the 1600s; top storey added in the late 1800s.
Same record, from the fire insurances: a large renovation between 1768 and 1773 (new ground-floor windows, new room layout, new render).

quote: ägdes och beboddes under 1600-talets senare del av kamreren Bengt Hansson. Från hans tid finns några murar och takdekorationer bevarade.
note: The whole block is one building. Walls and ceiling decorations survive from its later-1600s owner, so the house shows as later 1600s in origin.

quote: Han lät totalt ombygga husen och förse dem med vacker och präktig inredning
note: G. H. Conradi bought the whole block early in the 1750s and had the houses totally rebuilt. Facades 1860 and 1869, modernised 1969.

The museum's card: in 1966 medieval facade walls were recorded up to four storeys toward Österlånggatan / Köpmanbrinken (a 1940 note of medieval cellar walls is uncertain). The block article does not mention the house.

The museum's 2003 facade note: medieval walls in monk bond in the long walls of the vaulted ground-floor room (recorded 1987); an anchor of 1600s type higher up. The 1940s card (SSM_DOK_000813 p. 23) says medieval walls were reportedly found in the 1945-46 rebuild, undocumented.

quote: Efter 1762 var Stjärnan inrymd en trappa upp i en nyuppförd byggnad vid Österlånggatan 45
note: Corner of Österlånggatan 45 and Packhusgränd. The Källaren Stjärnan article: after 1762 the cellar, on this plot since 1602, was in a newly built house at no. 45; read as the 1760s, since the article gives no year it was finished.

quote: Bostadshuset Packhusgränd nr 6 är resultatet av en omfattande ombyggnad som utfördes 1939 efter ritningar av arkitekt Gunnar Morssing.
note: In 1939 the Packhusgränd 6 part, an older separate plot, was extensively rebuilt to Gunnar Morssing's drawings (the block article says pulled down and replaced). The corner house at Österlånggatan 45 is the post-1762 house.

The museum's 2006 report: medieval walls three storeys high in the alley facade (recorded 1970), and the stone houses here not built before well into the 1400s. A stone house in a 1661 deed; the passage over the alley named in 1550 (p. 4).
Same report: a new owner rebuilt the house in 1679; cellar beams dated by tree rings to 1661. Swedish Wikipedia's ironmonger (1647-1682) and 'from the building year' passage fit this phase.

quote: Huset blev delvis påbyggd 1849 och fick då sitt nuvarande utseende.
note: Swedish Wikipedia: partly raised in 1849, when it got its present look.

2005 masonry report (register-linked): both street facades are block bond, probably built in the late 1600s (1675-1699, the card's 'late 1600s'); a 1682 fireback may mark the build. An earlier medieval house is not proven (the medieval wall inside may be the neighbour's).
Large rebuild about 1774: the fire insurance has new outer and partition walls for the whole top storey and attics (same report).

quote: Fasaden är dock från senare delen av 1700-talet.
note: The facade is from the later 1700s (block article), so read as 1750-1799.

quote: Husets våningar byggdes om 1960-70 och fick moderna lägenheter efter ritningar av arkitekt Georg Scherman.
note: Floors rebuilt as modern flats 1960-70 to Georg Scherman's drawings (block article, citing the 1969 permit drawings).

Built new in 1662 across two older plots, on medieval cellars: the buyer was to pull down the two old stone houses, and the whole structure still dates from 1662 (p. 4). The block article and museum card SSM_DOK_000257 p. 3 put medieval walls in the cellars.

In 1959 the ground floor's street front lost its old rough render for a smooth one, against the City Museum's view, and the present panelled doors were made. A photo caption on p. 6 says the 1960s; the text says 1959.

1976 facade renovation (register-linked card): medieval masonry in the street facade up to just over three storeys, with a corbel of moulded brick above the ground floor and a blind band. No later rebuild year given.

Card for this merged plot: a 1938 photo shows medieval monk-bond walls up to three storeys on the square facade, with a medieval window, and another medieval body by Svartmangatan. The block article's 1816 house and its 1937-39 rebuild follow as rebuilds.

quote: Nuvarande huset uppfördes 1816 på de medeltida källarvalven.
note: Present house built 1816 on the medieval vaults; it is the house the article says was rebuilt in 1937-39 under the cited permit drawings for this plot. The restaurant article's '1700s' mixes in the corner house next door (1795).

quote: Det byggdes fullständigt om 1937–1939, efter ritningar av arkitekt Otar Hökerberg
note: Completely rebuilt 1937-39 to Otar Hökerberg's drawings, when the present look and the restaurant came (block article).

quote: I den nordöstra delen återfinns rester av ett eller möjligen två medeltida hus
note: North-east part keeps remains of one or two medieval houses and a 1300s wall (block article); the card SSM_DOK_000258 p. 3 finds medieval cellars of probably two houses. The west part, built 1807 on older cellars, is shown as the rebuild. KulturNav: no year.

quote: Västra delen uppfördes 1807 på äldre källardelar.
note: The west part of the house was built in 1807 on older cellar parts (block article).

Card for this address: the total rebuild found medieval walls inside and in both facades, over three storeys on the street with blind bands and a medieval window; at least two medieval houses. The lane overbuilding is dated 1570 (not shown).
Completely rebuilt in 1964-67, the card's survey years.

quote: är ett medeltida borgarhus som byggdes om vid 1600-talets mitt
note: Block article: a medieval burgher house rebuilt in the mid-1600s and again in 1780. The masonry card (SSM_DOK_000284 p. 3) has measured cellar walls only. Shown as medieval origin with its two rebuilds, the example the decision of 2026-10-20 gives.

quote: byggdes om vid 1600-talets mitt
note: Rebuilt around the mid-1600s (block article), read as 1640-1660; KulturNav's estimated 1600-1700 construction (49a4fd68) fits this rebuild.

quote: lät utföra ytterligare en ombyggnad år 1780
note: Rebuilt 1780 for the merchant Stutén, new facade by J. W. Friese (block article); KulturNav has a new facade 1779-81.
2015 museum report (register-linked) concludes the house reached about its present volume in the Middle Ages; medieval walls up to three storeys toward Prästgatan (1945). Owner records from 1484.
Rebuild applied for in 1768 (new tiled mansard roof, attic made a storey), still finishing when insured in 1787 (same report).
Larger rebuild in 1866 (new stair, Prästgatan wall raised), carried out the same year (same report).

Three old houses merged. 2004 report: medieval walls with a window reveal in the Köpmanbrinken house; c. 1600 walls in the Bollhusgränd house (also SSM_DOK_000623); the corner house on the square mostly early 1700s. Shown as origin plus rebuilds.
The corner house toward the square was partly built anew when the street was regulated between 1701 and 1733 (same report).
Large rebuild of the merged property in 1939 (same report).

Card: medieval walls in cellars at several levels, a medieval pier with window remains in the Österlånggatan facade, medieval walling above the south roof line. SSM_DOK_000715 finds none on the Baggensgatan side (two bodies, north one older). No rebuild year.

1959 facade renovation: medieval walls over four storeys on Österlånggatan, with five round-arched windows and a blind band; the 1972-73 rebuild showed the medieval house filled half the plot depth. Also in the museum's 1959 annual report.
Large rebuild in 1972-73 (same card).

1967 card for this address and corner (filed under the plot's older number): both street facades are medieval masonry their full length, up to three storeys, with original window and door remains. No rebuild year given.
The three lower storeys are medieval; at some point in the 1600s a further storey was added under a säteri roof. Wall anchors of the early 1600s show on the fronts.
The City's own records, as the sheet reports them, have a rebuild in the 1870s with a new stair and the säteri roof replaced. The 1914 insurance has the new stair but no roof change, so medium.
Complete rebuild in 1968: new roof truss, modern kitchens and bathrooms with some new partitions, and a refuse room off the street. Fits the museum card of 1967.

1963-65 inventory: medieval-character walls (monk bond) in the alley-side outer wall on ground, first and second floors (pp. 83, 108). Block article: a stone house on this plot sold in 1438. The footprint matches the corner house and wing.
Rebuilt and modernised 1963-65; the inventory was made for that work (title page).

Early 1600s: the plot's two medieval houses were joined and raised to four storeys, close to today's volume. Painted beam ceilings of about the 1620s survive (pp. 4, 8). Agrees with the medieval primary row.
Another rebuild around the middle of the 1600s gave the house new gables. A sandstone frieze of metopes on the street side is left from it.
A larger rebuild in 1815: bigger windows, the street gable rebuilt, a new plan, new joinery, stoves and plastered ceilings.

Part of the merged 'five small houses': this footprint holds the three western plots. Museum memo (1960): two stone houses named in a 1420 deed, and a 1420 stone house survives in the lower part of Nygränd 6, inside this footprint; a medieval corner on Österlånggatan (p. 3).
Two houses on one footprint (1982 inventory). The south house was built c. 1651-52 by the tailor Berleman (building under way 1651-52, p. 17). Its c. 1630 north neighbour was later pulled down.

North house built anew 1759-61 (cornerstone January 1759); at the same time the south house's top storey was replaced and its courtyard wing rebuilt from the ground, both houses four storeys (same inventory).

quote: Uppförande, Utförandeår 1630–1640, Uppskattat årtal
note: KulturNav's estimate for the wing of the von der Linde house (c. 1630, extended c. 1640 with the oriel); the 2019 report (p. 5) puts half the wing on this footprint, and KulturNav's point is inside it. Another house on the footprint beside the main house.

Scharenbergska huset, the main house on the square: built new, probably in the 1680s (2019 report, p. 5); Wikipedia (rev 55447690) says Scharenberg built it soon after buying in 1682 and moved the oriel onto it. The card is named for this house.
A fifth storey was added to both house and wing in the 1930s (same report).

1931 rebuild: medieval walls two storeys high along Kåkbrinken and in the lane overbuilding, with medieval window reveals. Wikipedia dates the overbuilding to the 1500s (a late-1500s wall painting); the museum thinks it is as old as the house.
Rebuilt and raised in the 1600s, when the overbuilding's street wall was replaced (same document, 1935 article).
Rebuilt in 1931, when the medieval walls were recorded (same card).

Frans Carré's house. The museum's 1986-87 facade study dates the monk-bond walls, up to four storeys toward Trångsund, to the 1500s, with 1500s glazed tiles laid in as it was built; the card (SSM_DOK_000254 p. 3) says medieval too. Renovated in the 1750s.

Museum card (1974): medieval masonry in the ground floor only, a medieval opening in the street front by the vaulted lane and monk bond in the shop's south wall; upper storeys undated. Ground-floor walls are enough for a medieval origin (second read).

Three storeys in the 1695 sale record, four at the first fire insurance of 1750, one storey more as the sheet notes; it gives no year for the raising, so the span is the window between the two records.

The east part with the stair house was added in the 1840s where a small stone house stood by the lane (p. 4). The history on p. 7: applied for in 1834, drawings revised in 1842, probably done by 1843, up to the street house's height.

Museum card (1965): several medieval plots merged; toward Prästgatan the medieval walls of a three-bay house at least three storeys high, the south Prästgatan house likewise, and monk bond up to three storeys in the courtyard front on Skomakargatan.

Museum card (1972 rebuild): medieval monk bond in the ground floor's north and east walls, with a blocked medieval window; a 1942 photo shows monk bond up to the 3rd floor in the courtyard front. No medieval work in the cellar.
1981 facade study: medieval monk-bond masonry nearly three storeys high in the street front, from two medieval phases; no medieval openings left. Shop openings c. 1900.
Raised to four storeys, with new floor beams and a red-painted brick front, probably in the first half of the 1600s (the memo dates it by anchors and brickwork).
The rear wing along the east and south plot lines, inside this footprint, was probably built in the 1600s, perhaps in two stages: its two parts have different floor levels.

New fronts and roof were applied for in 1767; the fire insurance first records the change in 1791. The courtyard wall was raised to add a half storey with four rooms, the roof was changed and the stair was laid in stone to the attic.

In 1799 the owner reported a new roof structure and renewed fireplaces, ceilings, panelling, doors and windows in every room. By then the street entrance had moved from the old west gateway to the east.

Corner house at Svartmangatan. 1993 survey: medieval-type monk bond in the front on the 1st and 2nd floors; the card (SSM_DOK_000281 p. 26) has medieval walls in cellars and up to the 3rd floor. Wikipedia's group line puts Kindstugatan 2-18 at c. 1600-1700.

The Cepheus history reprinted in the museum's report: the medieval corner house got an extra storey and a new broken roof in the 1750s, replacing its turf-covered lean-to roof; renovated throughout 1878.
1984 facade renovation (memo 1985): medieval-type monk bond in two piers of the street front, the north one four storeys high, with part of an original window and a putlog hole.
Top storey raised and one more storey added after an 1837 permit application; the memo says the work was done by the autumn insurance of '1938', evidently 1838.

Museum card (1959 facade restoration): medieval monk-bond masonry up to three storeys toward the street, with traces of painted decoration; the ground floor's north wall is monk bond throughout. Newer masonry above.

1982 facade survey: the four-storey front toward Järntorget is mostly well-laid, red-painted brickwork of 1600s type with its 1600s window openings; three bays toward Västerlånggatan are younger. KulturNav's entry has no date.

quote: Schantzska huset är en byggnad på Stortorget 20 intill Seyfridtzska huset i Gamla stan, Stockholm, uppförd 1650 och restaurerat 1905.
note: The red stepped-gable Schantz house (Stortorget 20), built in 1650 on medieval walls (SSM_DOK_000260 p. 3); KulturNav c148ddca estimates 1650 too. The card's name, photo and article are this house's, so it dates the footprint; the 1520s Seyfridtz house is its also row.

quote: Seyfridtzska huset är en byggnad på Stortorget 18 i Gamla stan, Stockholm, uppförd på 1520-talet.
note: The yellow Seyfridtz house (Stortorget 18), built in the 1520s; the museum card (SSM_DOK_000260 p. 3) has medieval walls over three storeys in its front. The City's data draws it and the Schantz house as one footprint, so it is the card's other house.
In 1861 the three houses got one shared entrance from Stortorget, and the western house on Solgränd was partly pulled down and partly rebuilt to the floor levels of its neighbour.
The 1904-05 rebuild joined the three houses for good: one new stairwell, the southern house's courtyard built over by a storey, services put in and the facades restored with small-paned windows.

Museum card for the house at Köpmangatan 8 / Peder Fredags gränd: medieval cellars of several house bodies, and the lane front has medieval masonry up to three storeys in places. This 5 x 26 m footprint runs along the lane's west side.

Museum card (1977 rebuild): two medieval stone houses joined; the older east one keeps four storeys of medieval masonry to the north and three to the south, the west one three to both lanes, with medieval windows and a cellar stair.

The sheet agrees the plot held two separate medieval houses (medieval brickwork survives through the third storey and partly above) and dates their probable joining, by a shared stairwell, to the first half of the 1700s.

quote: Dagens tre tullhus med nummer 1, 2 och 3 (från norr till söder) uppfördes åren 1939 till 1941 efter ritningar av arkitekt Paul Hedqvist.
note: Customs pavilion no. 3, the southernmost on the quay: this footprint is 33 x 13 m, the size the article gives for no. 3, and lies south of no. 2 (already dated). Paul Hedqvist; the article calls no. 3 unaltered.

quote: På 1750-talet uppfördes i kvarteret ett stort magasin för ett av stadens sockerbruk.
note: One footprint for the whole block. Its oldest part is the 1750s sugar-refinery store toward Lilla Nygatan (KulturNav: 1700-1800, estimated); a north wing followed in 1819.

quote: Nästa stora utbyggnad skedde mellan 1876 och 1877 då den lägre, nuvarande byggnadskroppen mot Mälartorget uppfördes
note: The lower body toward Mälartorget and a matching south wing, 1876-77, when the courtyard houses came down; Albert Törnqvist also rebuilt the older Lilla Nygatan part with its present facade.

The 1983-84 inventory (register-linked; BY-NC-SA, so cited as a report): medieval in origin except the top storey, with rare medieval rib vaults. The card (SSM_DOK_000285 p. 40) has medieval walls over three storeys toward Västerlånggatan.
Raised a storey under a manor-style roof in the second half of the 1600s (inventory summary); that roof gave way to the present one in 1856.

Museum card (1958-59): cellars of two medieval houses, and a monk-bond wall on the 3rd floor (the south fire wall or a spine wall). The articles are about residents (the Myrdals, the Palmes) and give no build year.

quote: Kammarkollegiet, Slottsbacken 6, byggt 1675, ombyggt 1909
note: The Coin Cabinet / Kammarkollegiet building. The Slottsbacken article's list of houses gives built 1675, rebuilt 1909; the Skomakare-Källaren article says the 1680s (the other either row).

quote: Byggnaden har sina rötter i 1680-talet då det uppfördes för den förmögne fransmannen Honoré Boneau.
note: Skomakare-Källaren article: built in the 1680s for Honoré Boneau; by the 1700s a main house with two wings toward Slottsbacken; bought by the shoemakers' guild in 1780.

quote: År 1780 förvärvades byggnaden av Skomakareämbetet som lät bygga om det 1805.
note: Rebuilt 1805 for the shoemakers' guild, which ran its Skomakare-Källaren restaurant in the west wing until 1903.

quote: Kammarkollegiet, Slottsbacken 6, byggt 1675, ombyggt 1909
note: Rebuilt 1909 per the Slottsbacken article; KulturNav (7d37e83d) dates Ferdinand Boberg's rebuild and extra storey to 1906-07 instead.

Museum card: medieval walls in the cellars of the Baggensgatan half, and the museum's 1959 report recorded a medieval three-storey house at Österlånggatan 24 whose gable became the neighbour's wall. The 1762-67 'brothel' is its fame, not its date.

Grevesmühl house. Nordberg's history in the museum's 1958 report: the merged plot's older houses largely gave way to Joakim Fult's rebuilding and new building begun in 1726; medieval and early-1600s walls survive in parts. Interiors finished after 1753.

Some time in the 1800s (no year given) the corner part lost its flat roof and railed terrace to a tall lean-to roof, changing the top of the house. The lower attic was fitted out in 1864, an interior step not counted here.

Medieval house: the museum's masonry card (survey 1970-71) finds a medieval building on the north half of the plot, monk-bond brick in both street and courtyard fronts up to the later eaves. The south half came later (next row).
An extension rather than a rebuild: the same card says the south half of the plot was probably built on in the first half of the 1600s.

The German School's house. The 1983 inventory (register-linked): after 1653 the school house was rebuilt or built new, probably both, as a 1670 portal witnessed; early-1600s walls may survive. Medieval remains only in the cellars.
Extended: after the plot took its final shape in 1744, the north part on Själagårdsgatan and the north courtyard wing were built; insured in 1747 as four storeys.
A new school building on the west part of the plot in 1775, paid for by a bequest (drawings by J. W. Dimling, not followed in detail).
Rebuilt into flats in 1886-87 after the school left; the inventory (p. 17) says this rebuild wiped out most earlier traces, so it looks like an 1880s house today.

quote: Huset ägdes på 1400-talet av Sten Sture den äldre.
note: Mäster Olofsgården. Standing in the 1400s, owned by Sten Sture the Elder, so a medieval origin rather than a build year; given to Pontus De la Gardie in 1576. The block article (rev 54655039) says the same.

quote: 1620 byggdes det om och på 1800-talet skedde ytterligare två ombyggnader.
note: Rebuilt in 1620; two more rebuilds in the 1800s, with no years given. The museum's 1981 masonry sketch (SSM_DOK_000631) has no readable date for the house.

Medieval house: the museum card (surveys 1940-58) finds a medieval building at the south corner, its walls at least two storeys high on both street fronts, with a clear joint to a later, undated part to the north. Jakob Bagge owned it in the late 1500s.

Medieval house: the museum card records medieval monk-bond masonry to just over four storeys in all three street fronts, and inside, found during a full rebuild in 1940. The article's later burgher houses stood on the back street, not this corner.

quote: uppfört kring 1640 för Fredrik Gustavsson Stenbock och hans hustru Katarina De la Gardie
note: The Stenbock palace, built about 1640 (building work through the 1640s; KulturNav estimates 1640-1650). The old national archive of 1887-90 shares the footprint: its also row, another house, not a rebuild.

quote: den omfattande till- och ombyggnad som Fredrik Stenbocks son, riksmarskalken Johan Gabriel Stenbock, lät utföra under åren 1661—1671
note: Its look today comes from the big extension and rebuild for Johan Gabriel Stenbock in 1661-71, led by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder (KulturNav: 1666-1671).

quote: Uppförande, Utförandeår 1887–1890, Exakt datering
note: The old national archive (Axel Fredrik Nyström), joined to the palace on this footprint: another house, not a rebuild. Wikipedia (rev 58964062) agrees on 1887-1890; the Riddarholmen list says 1877-90.

Medieval origin: the 1983 inventory's foreword (register-linked) says the house is medieval in its lower parts, its east wall probably on the 1200s town wall. A check in 2000 on the Prästgatan front (SSM_DOK_000651) found medieval walling on 1 tr and probably 2 tr.
Raised to its present height in the second half of the 1600s, with its säteri roof (the inventory's foreword). Cellar timber was felled after 1345 (SSM_DOK_000732), a fabric date only.

The museum card (1972-73): the house's own medieval cellars, and its original west wall medieval to over four storeys. Medieval origin; the street front and the courtyard wing came later (the 1632 row).

A sandstone cartouche over the street door bears 1632 and the then owners' initials; the sheet takes it as the likely year of a major rebuild. The museum card SSM_DOK_000807 p. 39 has the street front and courtyard wing without medieval walling, probably 1600s: this rebuild.

A grocer who owned this house and the one next door started rebuilding in 1760, probably a new roof with rooms fitted in the attic; the August 1761 insurance suggests the work was done. The sheet links the plain rendered front and the roof shape to it.

This house's own sheet has the renovation planned in 1970 (part of the cellar collapsed, foundations strengthened, new kitchens and bathrooms). The neighbour's sheet (also p. 8) says the City renovated three adjoining houses, this one included, together, done in 1974.

Medieval origin: the museum card (1959/65) finds medieval masonry in several building bodies; the oldest, on Köpmangatan, stands to over two storeys (three original floors). The 1963-65 inventory's mixed walls agree. The 1570 alley vault is not used.

The sheet puts a larger rebuild of the street house, read from its masonry, before the alley bridge passed to the neighbour by a 1673 deed, and ties the grisaille ceiling of the later 1600s (p. 10) to the same work: the second half of the 1600s, probably before 1673.

Work on the house began in 1963 with heavy repairs to its frame; the one-storey link wing between the street house and the courtyard house, inside this footprint, was pulled down and rebuilt (the sheet's plan, p. 3, marks it new in the 1960s).

The 1995 inventory: the NE street block possibly 1640s, the SE street house later 1600s; the property took its present form toward 1700 (p. 5). The later wings are the next rows (principle of 2026-10-20 instead of the hold).
An added house: the west stone house on Yxsmedsgränd was possibly built early in the 1700s (the inventory's 'possibly'; the card's 'early 1700s'); early-1700s cornices survive inside.
The north courtyard wing was built new in the 1780s, matching the surviving drawing of 1785, with a new cellar that year.

The museum card (1979): the medieval houses were probably pulled down after the 1625 fire and today's house built and finished about 1662, the year on its street portal. No medieval walling recorded; the cellars span the plot.

The 2002 facade report's conclusions: medieval monk-bond walling in the east parts of the cellars and none above ground, so a medieval origin (the cellar rule, as at Svartmangatan 17); the oldest walls above ground are late 1500s or first half of the 1600s by bond, brick and joints.
Anchor irons on the Funckens gränd front form LL, DL and 1627, read as Lydert Lang and his wife rebuilding the house then; the masonry dating of the walls above ground (p. 5) agrees.
1963 card: medieval masonry up to the third floor in the street and courtyard fronts, an intact medieval door and traces of six windows; a medieval courtyard house stood behind. Medieval origin.

The same card: the two southernmost window bays of the street front were added in the 1600s, an extension of the medieval house (the card's 'rebuilt or extended in the 1600s'; restored 2026-10-20, as the other extensions are shown).
1983 inventory summary: two houses joined by a wing. The Skomakargatan house keeps medieval masonry in the cellar and, in places, up to one storey; a stone house stood here by 1629. Medieval origin.

The Prästgatan house, built shortly before the mid-1600s by the owner who bought the plot in 1634 and sold it, much dearer, in 1651 (same inventory, pp. 5-6). A second house on this footprint, not a rebuild of the first.

quote: Det förmodas att husets källare härstammar från medeltiden medan de övre våningsplanen är av yngre datum.
note: The block article names this house by number and address: its cellar is thought to be medieval, the floors above younger and undated. Shipped as medieval origin; the cellar is the only dated part.

Two plots merged in the 1880s. In the eastern plot's Kindstugatan front the 1976 survey found medieval masonry about two window bays wide from a house of at least two storeys, and probably medieval cellars. Medieval origin.
The corner plot (Brända tomten/Kindstugatan) was regulated in the 1740s, after a fire, and built anew; its walls are homogeneous with much reused brick (1976 report).
1975 facade restoration card: medieval masonry with struck joints up to the third floor (2 tr) of the street front; no original openings found. Medieval origin.

1973 rebuild card: the plot runs through the block with a medieval house at each street. Skomakargatan front medieval to 2 tr plus large parts of the cellar; Svartmangatan front medieval in two phases over three storeys (p. 11).
The sheet reads wall anchors of 1600s type in the Svartmangatan and courtyard fronts as a rebuild of the medieval houses in that century (also the p. 7 caption). It gives no year.
Raised by one storey in 1748 for the owner of the time; the attic, with its storerooms and hoist winches, survives from then. The fire insurance of 1750 already gives today's volume (p. 6).

Card from surveys 1959-74: medieval masonry on floors 1-2 tr of the three southern bays toward Tyska brunnsplan, along the whole ground-floor front on Baggensgatan, and two medieval phases inside. Medieval origin.

1978 survey of the Helga Lekamens gränd front: no medieval masonry; the front probably rose in stages in the 1600s and 1700s. Lower joists carry mid-1600s-type anchors and the plinth may be 1600s, so ≈ the 1600s.

In 1758 a master joiner rebuilt the Helga Lekamens gränd house and added its top storey, with stone stairs and a stone-framed doorway. This dates the later top storey the 1978 museum memo found (its 1700s rebuilt row), so it takes that row's place.

The Göran Hälsinges gränd house, which the City draws in the same footprint: a stone house put up in place of plank sheds (still on a 1651 map) in the second half of the 1600s, judged by its 1600s wall anchors.

quote: Byggnaden uppfördes i slutet av 1630-talet eller i början av 1640-talet av riksrådet Peder Eriksson Sparre.
note: The Sparre palace (Birger Jarls torg 11): late 1630s or early 1640s, stored as 1635-1644, which the card words as the article does (the map's year, 1644, is the short-span rule's). Wings added in the 1700s. Kammarrätten's house of 1804 shares the footprint (also row).

quote: Byggnaden uppfördes 1804 för Kammarrätten i Stockholm efter Riddarholmsbranden 1802 på platsen för Kammarrättens föregående hus, det nedbrunna Cruuska palatset.
note: Kammarrättens hus (Birger Jarls torg 13): a new house of 1804 on the site of the palace burnt in 1802. The City's data draws it and the Sparre palace as one footprint: another house, not a rebuild of the palace.

quote: Från 1807 till 1808, efter den stora Riddarholmsbranden 1802, försågs det Sparreska palatset med ännu en våning.
note: After the 1802 fire the Sparre palace itself was raised a storey in 1807-08 (same article as the build year).

Card (survey 1940s): medieval masonry over the whole cellar plan. Cellar only; the house above is undated. The block barely escaped the 1625 fire, and the block article calls the next house, Yxsmedsgränd 2, of medieval origin on like evidence.

2004 report: the 1753 court valuation says the stone house had been rebuilt from the ground (drawings 1753); medieval-type walls survive at both party lines (p. 7). The 1976 facade report (SSM_DOK_000285 p. 9) reads the front as 1700s, keeping the old fire walls.

2000 interior card: monk-bond brickwork along the whole north wall of the ground-floor shop and in the cellar, later patched; the 2004 report next door finds medieval masonry in the same wall. Ground floor and cellar only. Medieval origin.

quote: Huset kallas Ehrencreutzska huset eller Tessinhuset som uppfördes på 1660-talet, troligen efter ritningar av Nicodemus Tessin d.ä.
note: The Stora Nygatan house (Ehrencreutzska huset): 1660s, probably by Tessin the Elder; rebuilt and refurnished in the 1760s. The 1989 inventory agrees (plot empty 1651, bought 1661).
1989 inventory: from 1759 the owner pulled down and rebuilt both courtyard wings and built a wholly new house on Lilla Nygatan, still unfinished at the September 1761 insurance.

Card from the 1972-73 full rebuild: medieval masonry of several periods; the courtyard walls are medieval up to six storeys, shared with the neighbours; nothing medieval in the street front. Medieval origin.

The inscribed stone over the door is dated 1643 and names the owner couple. The sheet thinks they may have rebuilt the house then, and the facade anchors of the early 1600s back this. The source hedges, so medium.
The fire insurance records the owner's rebuild of 1793: new floors, doors, windows and a new roof. No permit drawing survives.

The City renovated the house with its neighbours from the early 1970s and finished in 1974: new kitchens and bathrooms, with the cellar shored up. This fits the museum card made during the 1972-73 rebuild.

quote: är en medeltida byggnad med källarvalv och delar av bottenvåningen från 1336.
note: Medieval origin: the block article dates the cellar vaults and part of the ground floor to 1336; the house article (rev 59182697) calls it probably the house King Magnus Eriksson had built in 1336, perhaps Stockholm's oldest surviving dwelling.

quote: Även husets murverk härstammar troligen från den här perioden.
note: The house article: the high brick vaults of the ground floor and the house's masonry probably date from the 1590s, when King Sigismund bought it (1594) for Catholic services.

quote: En eldsvåda 1770 skadade huset, vilket en minnestavla i porten visar.
note: A fire in 1770 damaged the house; the Baggensgatan front probably got its present look in the repair.

1973-75 card: a big plot merged from several; medieval masonry only along the south boundary (cellar to 2 tr) and in the south part of the Österlånggatan front, over two storeys, with a medieval window. Partial: the rest is undated.

Measured at the 1937 rebuild: medieval masonry over four storeys high in the courtyard wing and in the street house (ground floor and 2 tr); in 1951 a medieval street front with a blind band was seen. Medieval origin.
Rebuilt 1937 (same card); the block article's 1936-37 clean-up to Albin Stark's drawings.

Card: merged from at least two medieval plots; the building at Gåsgränd has medieval monk bond over the full height of the passage's west wall (vaulted in the 1600s) with three niches, and the medieval house's south wall. Medieval origin.

No address: the corner at Västerlånggatan/Storkyrkobrinken, where the register links this 1992 inventory. Today's house was founded in 1652 (cellars dug then) with three storeys; a fourth before 1730.
Thorough 1758 rebuild: attic storey under a new roof, stone stairs (same inventory).
Rebuilt 1908 for offices and shops to a builder's design, giving today's exterior and interior (same inventory).

Cellar-only: the card for this address (1970) finds walls in monk bond of medieval type in a beam cellar in the east part of the plot; the west cellars are probably not medieval. Nothing above ground is dated.

quote: De första källarvalven, som så småningom började användas som vinkällare, byggdes sannolikt någon gång under 1300-talet.
note: Cellar-only: the block article puts the Stralsund cellar's first vaults probably in the 1300s and the house above them later, with no year. It gives the address as Skottgränd 9; this footprint is that property's only one.

quote: På Stora Nygatan 34 finns medeltida byggnadsrester i husets källare.
note: Cellar-only: the block article names this address and finds medieval building remains in its cellar; nothing above ground is dated.
Cellar-only: the 2009 report (register-linked) finds medieval masonry in some of the unplastered cellar walls; mid-1600s-type wall anchors in the facades, but no year for the house above.
Same report: a larger repair in the 1770s built the stone stairs up to the attic and gave the rooms plaster ceilings and new fireplaces.

The house on the quay went up around the mid-1600s, three storeys with carved gables; its sandstone portal is of that time (also p. 4). Read as 1640-1660. Wikidata's 1648, shown now, lies inside it, so s02 keeps 1648 (cited_period_vs_record).

In 1742 the house got a low fourth storey and a tall mansard roof, drawn by a master mason with a rusticated ground floor and pilasters; two stone shop booths and an outside stair were built in front.
A rebuild in 1837 extended the house into the courtyard to give the flats entrance halls, and the quay front got rendered mouldings.
After a fire in 1847 the top storey was raised, an attic flat fitted and the present roof built. 1847 is the fire's year; the sheet gives no separate year for the work that followed it.
A thorough renovation with underpinning from the mid-1970s: new layouts, offices below and flats above, the stairs recast in concrete; finished and inspected in 1981 (p. 8). Mid-1970s read as 1975.

The warehouse on the inner, west part of the plot (no. 2 on the sheet's plan), inside this footprint: built in 1786 after half the north wing and a store were pulled down, and little changed since (also p. 4).

A building stood on this street front by the mid-1400s; its cellar, and perhaps walls, survive in the north part of the street house. The south part's cellar is medieval too, its age above unknown. RAÄ gives the 1450s.
The parish bought the property in 1846 and rebuilt it as a school the next year, with two large classrooms on each floor. The rebuild is told on p. 7, and p. 8 names 1847.
In 1864 the street house's top storey was raised to its present height, with a new roof frame and a saddle roof.
A rebuild into flats began in 1944, part of the old town's renewal. The summary on p. 4 says the 1940s and p. 8 says 1940; the year here is the history section's.

The south courtyard wing: the 1746 fire insurance lists a three-storey stone wing with a cellar as newly built, two years after the plot was enlarged south. Its lower two storeys stand; the top ones went in the 1940s.
A tobacco maker who owned the property in 1800, and sold it in 1807, raised the wing by a storey and gave its roof dormers for his works. That storey went again in the 1944 rebuild.
In the 1847 school conversion each upper floor of the wing got a large classroom (p. 7); later in the school years its two lower floors became gym halls.
In the rebuild begun in 1944 the wing's two top storeys were taken down and it became a communal laundry; artists' studios followed from 1979.

Stadsholmen's sheet records medieval walling in the cellars (pp. 4 and 6). Under the cellar rule that dates the house's origin; the house above took its present height and form when it was raised in 1755 (the rebuilt row).

Raised in 1755 for the owner of the time, to a master mason's drawings, giving today's four storeys and mansard roof. P. 8 calls 1755 the house's building year, but pp. 4 and 6 describe a rebuild of an older house.

The sheet finds medieval walling in the cellars, in the ground floor towards Baggensgatan and three storeys up towards the courtyard (also p. 4): medieval at its core. Main house and wing had today's volume by the 1759 insurance and the 1761 survey (p. 6).

1839: the street front was redecorated as it is today and given tall round-headed windows for the synagogue hall, whose ceiling was raised at the same time (also pp. 4 and 7). A new facade on the older house.

The City bought the house in 1912 and rebuilt it late in that decade: a new stair, the narrow courtyard house pulled down and the courtyard built over at ground level (p. 7). No year is given, so the 1910s.
House no. 1 on the sheet's plan, along Tyska Skolgränd from Svartmangatan (the footprint's addresses match): medieval masonry is recorded in its cellar and three storeys above ground. No year.
The sheet reads the 1600s-type wall anchors as a raising of the house in that century.

In the block's clearance in the 1930s part of the house was pulled down to light the courtyard, leaving only the ground floor of its three eastern bays. P. 10 puts the demolition in 1939; a 1938 photo (p. 5) already shows it.

Mostly house no. 2 on the sheet's plan, at Svartmangatan and Tyska Brunnsplan: medieval masonry in its cellars and three storeys above ground. The footprint also holds the southern of the two medieval houses on Själagårdsgatan (p. 10).
A fourth storey and a säteri roof (a roof with a low upright break) were added in the 1600s or the first half of the 1700s, the sheet says.
The roof toward the square took its present shape, with dormers, in the 1870s (p. 10 says the same of the neighbouring part on Själagårdsgatan).
In the 1939 clearance the house was extended about 4 m into the courtyard on every floor, absorbing its small east wing; the plan (p. 3) marks the extension.

House no. 1 on the sheet's plan, at Lilla Nygatan and Kåkbrinken: a three-storey stone house the city's master builder put up in the 1690s. The footprint also holds the 1754 wing (no. 2), a little longer on Kåkbrinken (seven bays to five); the street house leads.
The low wing along Kåkbrinken to Munkbrogatan (no. 2 on the plan) was added in 1754, when a goldsmith owner had the house rebuilt; the City draws it and the corner house as one footprint.
In 1754 a goldsmith owner had the corner house rebuilt to an architect's drawings, partly with new interiors.
A thorough rebuild in 1854, mainly toward Kåkbrinken and Munkbrogatan: the wing gained a third storey and the facades their present rusticated ground floor and arched shop windows.
In the 1970s rebuild a narrow new body (no. 3 on the plan) was joined to the house toward Kåkbrinken; p. 10 dates the whole property's renovation to the early 1970s.
House no. 4 on the plan, Lilla Nygatan 10: a smith built a stone house on the street in the 1690s. The sheet says its first look is unknown but it is probably today's house, hence medium.
The whole property was thoroughly rebuilt in the early 1970s with the City Museum advising: facades kept, plans changed for kitchens and bathrooms, the light well behind this house built over.
House no. 5 on the plan, Munkbrogatan 9: built in 1784 to an architect's drawings, four storeys with a north wing and a one-storey stable range to the south.

House no. 6 on the plan, at Lilla Nygatan and Schönfeldts gränd: a sculptor bought the plot in 1692 and built the stone house, first of three storeys (p. 6: the street's stone houses went up in the 1690s). Medium: Wikipedia has his standing house built later, undated.
Raised by a storey in 1778, when a cannon-founder owner carried out larger building works on the plot.
The street facade, with decorated pilasters and a rusticated ground floor, comes from a rebuild in 1872.
Rebuilt with the rest of the property in the early 1970s; the simpler courtyard facade of the first house was then partly reconstructed (p. 9).

The 1746 owner asked to build the house new from its foundations; the sheet does not know if older walls were kept, but the present size and layout match that design. A stone house with a vaulted cellar is recorded on the plot by 1511, so this replaced an older house.

A rebuild in 1831 under a later owner: stone stairs laid from the cellars up to the first upper floor and the stair moved nearer the street door. The 1860s cast-iron stair and the 1971 and 2011 renovations are not counted as rebuilds.

Traced to 1628, when a stone house here was sold; called old and decayed in 1677. The facade anchors are 1600s and the sheet cannot say if the house was built or rebuilt then (a caption leans to a rebuild), so about the 1600s, perhaps on an older core.

Raised one storey to four between 1835 (no changes noted since the 1757 insurance) and the 1837 fire insurance, which already shows it; the summary page says the 1830s. A cast-iron stair followed in 1891.

Medieval origin: medieval masonry in the middle of the three vaulted cellars (p. 7) and brick that seems laid in medieval bond in the ground floor (p. 10); nothing says the older houses went, and parts of the frame are probably older than its 1600s volume (p. 4).

Three small plots (half-timbered houses, perhaps a small stone house, on the 1651 map) were raised and joined into today's four-storey house before 1700, going by uniform 1600s-type anchors on every floor (pp. 6-7, 10).

The small courtyard house by Bollhustäppan: the old range here was pulled down in 1960 for the park and this one-storey house built over its vaulted cellar, which the sheet dates to the 1400s; some street-side walls of a range of about 1700 may survive (pp. 4, 8).

Medieval house: medieval masonry at least two storeys up in the wall to the closed alley, medieval wall anchors higher still and medieval walls in the cellar. The summary (p4) calls the house medieval.
Large rebuild of 1780 (a statement of 1781 lists the work): new floors, doors, windows and panelling, a fourth cellar vaulted, the gateway paved, two attic rooms. Much of its window joinery survives.
Large rebuild of 1942: a new stone stair on a concrete frame up to the attic, new flat doors, bathrooms and new kitchens, an air-raid shelter in the cellar and rooms made in the attic.

Medieval origin: the cellars keep medieval masonry from three separate earlier plots. Above them stand two houses with early-1600s front walls, joined into one in 1790 (lead, p. 4). Same reading as Funckens gränd 2 (medieval cellar, dated anchors a rebuild).

Wall anchors on the Prästgatan front spell 1630 in the southern of the two houses (also the caption, p. 5, and p. 7); the sheet puts the front walls in the early 1600s. Read as the rebuild above the medieval cellars.

Rebuilt in 1790 for a wholesaler: the two houses became one, with a shared gateway and stone stair, and the Prästgatan wall was raised so the lower attic became a full storey (p. 7, which says the work began in the 1790s).
A rebuild in the 1860s shaped most of today's interiors: new entrance portal and door, floor levels of the two halves evened out, new joinery and tiled stoves.
The ground-floor shops got a new front toward Västerlånggatan in 1899.

Medieval origin: the cellars join three or four medieval cellar systems and medieval masonry was recorded in the west part of the ground floor; written sources trace a street house back into the 1500s. Replaces the OSM 1760 tagged on the whole block.
A larger rebuild in the 1600s, read from the gateway's groin vault and the 1600s-type wall anchors on the street and alley fronts (p. 6 calls it probable).
A fifth storey added toward Österlånggatan around 1850, under a low lean-to roof.
The street front got its present look, moulded window surrounds and string courses, in 1878 (also p. 7).

Early-1600s masonry in the ground-floor shops; the sheet thinks the house possibly new-built then (its lead, p. 4: frame from the 1600s). Stone house first named 1646. Medieval anchors and a reused medieval stone occur but no medieval cellar or wall is reported.
The stair tower or the wing, both drawn in this footprint: in 1646 the records first name an attached house as newly built beside the stone street house.
A 1688 property deed describes three storeys with a bakehouse, the top storey then being rebuilt.
The street house reached its present height about 1750 when the top storey was added (caption; p. 9 too): three storeys in the 1748 insurance, four by the 1755 valuation (p. 7).
Rebuilding drawings of 1848, mainly for the wing and the courtyard houses: a new cellar stair and vaults and changes to the wing's joists and walls, probably for subsidence in the west part.
For the ironmonger's shop the gateway moved to its present south end in 1882, with iron spiral stairs, new shop windows and the ground floor's banded render (p. 9 says 1880; an earlier move in 1873).
Renovated 1980-81 with the house next door: the wing's joists replaced, new kitchens, bathrooms and partitions, every window replaced (pp. 6 and 9 say 1980, p. 8 1981).

The sheet dates the oldest parts of the present house, its walls and vaults, probably to the 1620s, built for a merchant (pp. 4, 6). The house was later raised and extended over the lane to its south.

The lane south of the house was built over from 1758 and done by 1762: the southernmost window bay of the lane facade, half the house deep (p. 9). A barrel-vaulted room in the south shop remains of it.
The owner applied in 1800 to raise the house by a half storey, and the work went on into the following year, so read as 1800-1801. Probably rooms for his servants.
Rebuilt in 1863 with partly new interiors. The lane facade got its plaster mouldings and window surrounds then (p. 5 gives the 1860s).
In 1935 the facade was simplified. The ground-floor rustication and the upper window surrounds and mouldings were removed, and the interior was renovated at about the same time.
The palace was built after the plot changed hands in 1694. The sheet gives the 1690s for the three lower storeys, and an engraving of 1702 shows it new (pp. 4, 6). This agrees with Wikidata's 1690s.
In the 1760s a new owner raised the main house one storey to its present height, lengthened the wings to the west and refitted the rooms in rococo style (p. 7; p. 8 says about 1760).
In the 1950s the rest of the block was demolished for a new road. The wing parts added around 1760 were cut off, the wings got new west gables and the facades were replastered (pp. 8, 10).

The one-storey courtyard range in the south-west corner (plan p3, no. 3). The 1917 courtyard house had sunk and was replaced by a low new range in the 1985 renovation. The building description (p10) says late 1900s.

The southern of two houses joined into one property in 1972. Both plots were built on by the late Middle Ages and keep medieval masonry in their cellars, and nothing says the older house went: a medieval origin. Much of its 1600s carcass survives (p. 4).
Rebuilt 1669-71 for a French cook, as his estate inventory of 1671 lists: walls, joists and attic seen to, tiled stoves and baking ovens put in, new windows; three storeys high afterwards.

Raised a storey under a new mansard roof for its grocer owners. The sheet's text puts this house in the south and the City Museum's register (records 49, 167) on Norra Dryckesgränd, as here; the plan (p3) swaps the numbers.

The northern of the two joined houses, on Södra Bankogränd (the sheet's text; the City Museum's register, record 167). Both plots were built on by the late Middle Ages and keep medieval masonry in their cellars, and nothing says the older house went: a medieval origin.
Much of its 1600s carcass survives (p. 4), and it had its stair projection on the lane by the early 1600s (p. 6); 1600s engravings show it three and a half storeys high with scrolled gables.
A pharmacist's widow applied to rebuild in 1740; by the 1756 insurance the stair had moved, the roof was a mansard and the gables were gone. The work's own year is not given, hence the span.

The sheet finds medieval masonry in the house (p. 4) and medieval cellars under the whole plot (p. 6) but gives no year, so the medieval span. Today's size and look come from the 1756 rebuild, which the sheet takes for a large rebuild rather than a new house.
Rebuilt to a drawing in 1756, from two storeys over a vaulted cellar to today's size and look. The owner called it a new house, but the sheet takes it as a large rebuild, not a demolition.
The sheet puts the house's building in the late 1500s, dated by wall paintings of that time and the ground-floor beams. It was a stone house by 1602 (p. 6). RAÄ's 1500s agrees, and this narrows it.

Rebuilt and raised in the first half or middle of the 1600s, read from the wall anchors and moulded beams. A raising line sits above the third floor, and the stepped gable belongs to the addition (p. 7).
A large rebuild, probably done by 1747. The owner, a stonemason, set up a portal with that year and insured the house the same year: four storeys over vaulted cellars.

The small three-storey courtyard house by Trädgårdsgatan (no. 4 on the plan, p. 3; matched by place, size and height) went up in the early 1600s with the yard wall. The 1610/1611 boundary splits the span, so it gets no colour.
